# About the house in Glenmore

I want to tell you all about the house in Glenmore myself, rather than have the news go around in bits on the phone. Some of you have already heard, and I’m sorry for how that happened. I should have spoken to the family properly before now.

I’ve agreed to sell the house. The sale was agreed on 3 November, and it is due to close on **15 January 2027**. I’m putting the date here plainly so that nobody has to hear it from somebody else again.

I know this will be hard news for some of you. It’s hard for me to write it. The house has been part of this family for longer than most of us have been alive, and I know it isn’t just mine in the way it lives in people’s memories. Before I say anything else, I want you all to know that I’d love to have a family day there on **Sunday 13 December**, before the house is cleared. Anyone who can come is welcome. I’ll have soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies.

I also want to tell you why I’ve made the decision, who is buying the house, and what we’re keeping. There are things I haven’t told you that I should have, and I’ll come to those too.

## The house and all that went with it

Glenmore was built in 1931 by Tom’s grandfather, Pádraig Mulkerrin. I don’t need to explain to most of you where it is, but for the younger ones reading this in Boston and Perth and Leeds, it’s near Oughterard, above the lake. It was the old Mulkerrin place, and it was where Tom grew up.

Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind the house in 1979. It was raining, of course, and the cattle were watching us. I can still see him there. I can’t remember what the cattle made of it, though I don’t think we impressed them very much.

Later on, the children learned to swim in the lake below the house. Declan used to refuse to come out until his lips were blue, no matter how many times we called him. I’m sure he’ll tell me I’ve got that wrong, but I haven’t.

Those are the kinds of things that come back to me when I think of Glenmore. Not the roof or the pipes or the papers to be signed, but Tom in the rain and the children down at the water. I know every one of you will have your own memories of the place. Some of you knew it before I ever did, and some only got there on visits when you were small. I hope we can talk about those days when we get together in December.

Since Tom died in March 2024, I’ve been driving out every fortnight to air the house and check the pipes. It’s forty minutes each way. At first I didn’t mind the drive. It was something that needed doing, and I was glad to see the place. But it has become harder to keep up with, and the house itself needs more than those visits can give it.

## Why I’m selling

In September, Ó Flaithearta’s surveyed the roof. There are slates to be dealt with and work needed on the back chimney. The quote came to €38,000. There is damp in the back bedroom as well, and the septic tank needs replacing to sell the house to anyone anyway.

I don’t want to make this sound as if I sat down with a list of repairs and decided overnight. The work and the cost are part of it, certainly, but they aren’t the whole story. Over the best part of two years I’ve been coming to terms with the fact that I cannot go on maintaining the house.

There’s something else I need to tell you. Last February, I slipped on the step at the back door when it was frosty. I lay there for twenty minutes before I could get up. I told nobody until now.

I know some of you will be cross with me for keeping that to myself, and you have every right to be. It frightened me. Since then I’ve been afraid of being alone at the house, even though I kept going out. It isn’t easy to admit that about a place where we have spent so much of our lives, but it’s true.

I know that selling Glenmore may feel sudden to those of you who haven’t been hearing what’s been going on. I should have told you about the fall and spoken more openly about the work the house needs. Instead, I kept much of it to myself while I was trying to work out what to do.

Over the best part of these two years, I have come to realise that I can keep Tom’s memory without keeping the house. That has taken me a long time to say, and longer to believe. Selling it doesn’t mean I love it any less, or that I’ve forgotten what it meant to him and to all of us.

Tom always said the house should have children in it, not be a museum. I’ve thought about that often.

## The family moving in

The buyers are a young couple, Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, and they have two small children. They want to live in the house; it won’t be a holiday let.

The price was fair. It was less than the Dublin crowd offered in the summer, and I took the lower offer on purpose. It mattered to me that a family would make their home there.

The Joyces have also said that the family can come out and walk the land any time. I was very glad of that, and I wanted you all to know it.

## What we’re keeping

We’re keeping the dresser, which is going to Úna’s. We’re also keeping Pádraig’s fiddle, the photographs, the Sacred Heart lamp and the gate sign.

I know those things can’t stand in for the house itself. But they belong with the family, and I’m glad they’ll still be with us. I hope, too, that we can look through the photographs together on the 13th and have a few arguments about who is who.

## Declan

I need to say something here to Declan, though I know he isn’t the only one who was hurt by the way this came out.

Declan, you heard from your cousin Gráinne on WhatsApp, not from me. You rang me at two in the morning your time, and you said I was “selling Dad”. I said things back that I shouldn’t have. I’m sorry for that, and I’m sorry you had to find out the way you did.

I regret not consulting you. I should have talked to you before it got to this point and listened to what you had to say. I understand why the news upset you, especially coming from somebody else.

I also need to be honest that I’m not willing to wait until your summer visit. I cannot manage the house any longer, and I’ve decided to go ahead with the sale. I’m sorry for how you found out, but I’m not sorry for making the decision.

I’m not angry with you, Declan. I love you, and the door is open. Whenever you’re ready to talk, I’m here.

## One more day together

For everyone who can make it, please come to Glenmore on **Sunday 13 December**. We’ll have soup and sandwiches, and there’ll be time to walk around, look at the photographs and spend a day together before the house is cleared. Bring wellies.

I know not everyone will be able to travel, especially those of you so far away. You’ll be with us in our thoughts, and I’d love to hear your memories of the house here on the blog, whether you can come or not. Úna set this up years ago so we could keep up with one another across all those miles, and I’m grateful for it now.

This is a sad thing in many ways. I won’t pretend otherwise. I’ll miss Glenmore, and I know you will too. But I’m glad another family will live there, and I hope their children will be as happy there as ours were.

With love to you all.
